The post West Coast Aligoté Shines appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known for kirs – cocktails made from dry white wine and crème de cassis – than fine wine. Today, it has become a darling of American wine connoisseurs.

As white burgundy prices have soared, Aligoté’s relatively modest cost, coupled with dramatic improvements in quality championed by dedicated advocates such as Sylvain Pataille and Aubert de Villaine, has fuelled an Aligoté renaissance, particularly in Bouzeron, the Burgundian village appellation specifically dedicated to the grape. These two producers, along with a band of Burgundians who call themselves Les Aligoteurs, have helped turn a grape valued as an occasional blending component or source of simple quaffing wine into a sought-after variety for serious white wines.

Not surprisingly, the rising star of Burgundian Aligoté has sparked producer interest in America. On 2 May, Balsall Creek winery in Oregon’s Willamette Valley held the Aligoté Affair, at which they and 11 other Oregon wineries poured their Aligotés for a sold-out crowd of 150. The event was billed as the first tasting dedicated to Aligoté in America. I couldn’t make it but the event did get me wondering just how many producers in Oregon and California were exploring the variety.

The answer? A lot more than I or anyone else expected.

title: Why South Africa is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part I

The post Why South Africa is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part I appeared first on Vinography.
content:
That’s not just a headline designed to attract attention. It’s my professional opinion as someone who tastes and writes about global wines for a living. I believe there is no more exciting wine region on the planet right now than South Africa.

There are plenty of reasons for that, from the country’s extraordinary old vineyards and geological diversity to the sheer quality and value of its wines. But if I had to put my finger on one thing that makes South Africa particularly special, it would be the country’s collaborative spirit.

That can sound very woo-woo or philosophical, but it represents a very real factor in the development and evolution of any wine region, and South Africa’s culture in that regard is something special.

If South Africa’s collaborative spirit had a set of poster children it would most certainly be the motley crew that call themselves the Zoo Cru (or most recently Zoo Corp – more on that in a moment). This collection of winemakers and their independent wine brands represents a distillation of everything that makes South Africa so fantastic right now, from their collective creativity to the quality of their wines, to the self-effacing energy they put into making wine actually… wait for it… fun.

Evolving a new wine culture

In the first half of the 20th Century, as it recovered from Phylloxera like the rest of the world, the South African wine industry distinguished itself by being heavily focused on brandy and fortified wines. It was dominated by large cooperative wineries that relied on a network of growers throughout the country supplying large quantities of grapes to make inexpensive table wines and spirits.

The imposition of apartheid in 1948 quickly led to international isolation and the drying up of international markets for South African wine. The industry languished during this time, relying on local markets and suffering through a lot of economic hardship. Towards the end of the apartheid period, some independent producers made investments of time and money to improve quality, and a few, like Kanonkop and Meerlust, began or returned to estate bottling.

Not until the end of apartheid, the democratic elections of 1994, and the removal of sanctions did the conditions emerge for South Africa’s modern fine-wine industry to truly take off. The first efforts in this regard were made primarily by these historic estates, who already owned the vineyards and possessed the capital required to improve quality, followed by newer independent producers who came with enough capital to get started in the business, usually by purchasing existing vineyards from long-time growers.

And then in 2000, a young man named Eben Sadie changed the trajectory of South African wine forever when he began making wines under his family name. Released a couple of years later, the initial vintages of Sadie Family Wines took the industry by storm, earning significant international critical acclaim and commanding prices that demonstrated a new ceiling for ambitious South African wine. Sadie owned no vineyards to begin with, instead choosing to establish contracts with growers of historic old-vine vineyards, paying a premium for farming to his exacting specifications.

Sadie’s near-overnight success made him a model for what the next generation of fine-wine production could look like, and as I related in my piece Tasting the Swartland Revolution, he and a couple of other producers also set the tone for the industry’s collaborative spirit. Young aspiring winemakers came knocking at his door, asking him how he did what he did, and he invited them in and showed them everything. Andrea and Chris Mullineux, as well as Adi Badenhorst, followed suit.

The result of the Swartland Revolution’s openness was twofold: a whole generation of young winemakers primed for open collaboration and collegiality, and a broadly shared set of ideas about how to make terroir-driven fine wine that showcased South Africa’s unique viticultural resources. Those ideas included seeking out old vineyards (thankfully still left in the ground from the co-op days) with South Africa’s heritage varieties, picking for acid retention and lower alcohol rather than ripeness, using ambient yeasts, aging in neutral oak or concrete, and, when appropriate, incorporating a healthy dose of whole clusters.

Putting the Cru in Zoo

Sadie and others like him proved to be powerful accelerants in the evolution of independent, boutique wine brands in South Africa. The proliferation of small winemaking projects in a growing market would not in itself be remarkable. Quite the contrary, it would be expected under the circumstances. What is so special about South Africa, however, is the staggering quality of so many of them.

There are not just a handful of world-class South African producers these days. There are dozens and dozens of them.

And a bunch of them like hanging out together.

“Myself, Chris Alheit, and John Seccombe were all renting space together,” says winemaker Peter-Allan Finlayson, who makes wines for his own brand Crystallum as well as Gabrielskloof. ‘I don’t think any of us were actually making that much wine. There was a lot of time for coffee and coffee breaks. So we got to talking about Cape Wine, and none of us wanted to have our own stand. We wanted to do something together, as sort of an umbrella for people like us making independent wines.”

The unlikely inspiration for the group’s original name came from Finlayson’s school days, courtesy of his favorite art teacher.

“She taught us about Basquiat and took us on the train to the center of Cape Town,” says Finlayson. “Time with her was just totally different than the rest of the school time.”

That art teacher, Diana Page, was part of a collective called the Boudoir Biscuits.

“That name just sort of stuck with me,” says Finlayson, “so we came up with the name The Zoo Biscuits. It was obviously generic enough, and we thought it was funny and kind of different from everything else that was out there. So we used that name for our first collective stand at Cape Wine. But then we got sued by the actual owners of the Zoo Biscuits trademark in South Africa when we tried to register our website. So then it became Zoo Cru, which was a little more grown-up anyway.”

Make no mistake, this isn’t some formal association of independent producers. There are no dues, no bylaws, not even a charter of any kind. It has organized itself spontaneously, first around friendship and second around a shared commitment to a certain approach to wine and a certain standard of quality.

“It was really just this umbrella under which we could do some fun things, and be together as friends and create a bit of interest,” says Finlayson.

The first time I encountered the Zoo Cru, the group was in its 70s glam disco era. After wandering through the staid, typically boring convention center architecture of booths, I rounded a corner to find a riotously colorful set of stands, staffed by the most outrageously dressed set of winemakers I’ve ever seen at a wine convention (see feature image at top). The Zoo Cru vibe was instantly infectious, and their corner of the massive national wine show was all but irresistible.

Membership in the group has been by invitation only, and has shifted over the past 10 years and three incarnations of the Cape Wine trade show. Some winemakers have left the group, and others have joined. Some invitations to join have not been accepted, says Finlayson, while some outside requests to participate have been declined by the group in service of preserving both their collegiality and their vibe.

Tired of the disco glam schtick, the group decided on a new incarnation for the most recent Cape Wine in 2025: Zoo Corp. They started with a two-hour video shoot (you really should see the videos) in the style of the TV show “The Office,” and ended up with a stand decorated in the style of 1960s corporate dystopia that would have made the art directors of Severance proud.

Such antics could easily be chalked up to a bunch of wacky winemaking friends with a desire to have a little fun. Who wouldn’t like a little more levity in their big convention hall? Taste the wines of the various members of this group, however, and you’ll immediately understand that these are some of the best winemakers in South Africa.

Wandering randomly around large wine tasting events where you are unfamiliar with the producers on offer generally proves to be an extremely hit-or-miss proposition. Stumble on the Zoo Corp stand, and you’d get one great wine after another in an astonishing progression through some of the best renditions of Chenin Blanc, Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, and Chardonnay that are made in South Africa.

This collection of friends represents so much of what makes South African wine exciting: incredible energy, an unwillingness to take themselves too seriously, and an unwavering commitment to expressing South Africa through world-class wines. Behind their chaotic, sometimes happenstance marketing collaboration lies a remarkably tight network of knowledge sharing, mutual respect, technical support, and genuine friendship. That kind of camaraderie, and the fun they have with it, is not common in the wine industry anywhere in the world.

Zoo Corp is not the reason I think South Africa is the most exciting wine region on the planet. They’re simply one particularly colorful manifestation of why: extraordinary talent working with extraordinary raw materials in a culture where ideas, knowledge, equipment, advice, encouragement, and apparently the occasional leopard print fuzzy vest are freely shared.

In Part II, I’ll look beyond the Zoo at some of the many other producers making an equally powerful case for South African wine. For now, here are 173 wines from this remarkable collection of friends.

Tasting Notes

White, Pink, and Orange Wines With a Score Between 9.5 and 10

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Huilkrans” Chenin Blanc, Citrusdal Mountain, Olifantsberg, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of orange peel, nectarine, struck flint, and dried herbs. In the mouth, stony orange peel, Asian pear, and a hint of unripe nectarine mix with pulverized quartz as fantastic acidity keeps things shining and vibrant across the palate. Faint salinity. A knockout. From red sand and clay soils at 440 m elevation with 50-year-old vines. 13% alcohol. Cost: $100. click to buy.

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Magnetic North” Chenin Blanc, Citrusdal Mountain, Olifantsberg, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, white peach, white flowers, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, white flowers, citrus pith, pear, and bee pollen flavors are crystalline and bright with fantastic acidity and a gorgeous silky length combined with a stony underbelly and faint salinity. Gorgeous. 45-year-old massale-selection vines grown at 540m elevation. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $108. click to buy.

2024 Damascene Chenin Blanc, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear and pear skin, wet chalkboard, a hint of pomelo, and white flowers. In the mouth, pomelo, pear skin, wet pavement, and white sage flavors are gorgeously bright with fantastic acidity, a chalky texture, and a deeply crystalline character. Stunning. From three soil types: granite, greywacke, and shale. All vineyards are above 325 m of elevation. 13% alcohol. Cost: $63. click to buy.

2024 Damascene Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine posesses an incredibly floral perfume of white flowers, Asian pear, lemon oil, and a hint of struck match. In the mouth, stony, crystalline lemon oil, white flowers, and pear flavors mix with crushed stone and wet chalkboard. Deeply stony and slightly saline. Gorgeous. 13% alcohol. Cost: $62. click to buy.

2023 Momento Grenache Gris, Voor-Paardeberg, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale peachy gold in the glass, this wine smells of peach, grapefruit, and a hint of watermelon. In the mouth, orange peel, nectarine, dried herbs, unripe apricot, and white flower flavors have gorgeous, shimmering acidity and deeply stony minerality. Outstanding. Seven days on the skins in a cold soak, then pressed and settled into old oak. 13% alcohol. Cost: $192. click to buy. (I’m not sure what is going on with that price, BTW).

2024 Rall “NOA” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, pear, Asian pear, and beeswax. In the mouth, stunningly bright lemon oil and Asian pear flavors are mouthwatering and salty with crystalline stony minerality and a faint rocky grip. Great depth and resonance. Aged in concrete and foudre. 13% alcohol. Cost: $48. click to buy.

2024 Savage “White” White Blend, Western Cape, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of apples, struck match, salty lemon, and white flowers. In the mouth, amazingly electric, saline lemon and grapefruit flavors have a faint chalky minerality and a lovely jasmine floral note. Gorgeous. A blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. 14% alcohol. Cost: $49. click to buy.

2021 Savage Wines “Savage White” White Blend, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of passionfruit and candied lemon. In the mouth, gorgeously bright lemon peel and grapefruit flavors are neon-bright, zippy, saline, and infused with crushed-stone minerality. Mouthwatering and impossible not to swallow. A blend of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $50.

White, Pink, and Orange Wines With a Score Around 9.5

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Fire By Night” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Bright yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, citrus oil, fynbos, and a hint of struck flint. In the mouth, saline flavors of Asian pear, lemon oil, dried herbs, and wet chalkboard are crystalline and wonderfully clear, with excellent acidity and length. Fabulous.12.5% alcohol. Cost: $75. click to buy.

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Nautical Dawn” Chenin Blanc, Polkadraai Hills, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, lemon oil, pomelo, and wet pavement. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon oil, unripe pear, yellow flowers, and fynbos are bright with fantastic acidity and a light stony grip. Gorgeous. 13% alcohol. Cost: $75. click to buy.

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Monument” Sémillon, Franschhoek, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light to medium yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, lemon oil, and a hint of yellow flowers. In the mouth, bright lemon oil and lemon peel flavors have a bright stony quality, with yellow herbs, crushed stone, and phenomenal crystalline minerality. Delicate, filigreed acidity. From vines planted sometime between 1900 and 1936 or earlier. 13% alcohol. Cost: $101. click to buy.

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Hemelrand Vine Garden” White Blend, Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, apples, and herbs. In the mouth, faintly saline flavors of apple, pear, yellow herbs, citrus pith, pomelo, and lime are deliciously bright, with fantastic acidity. Delicious and incredibly distinctive in character. A blend of 32% Roussanne, 28% Chardonnay, 25% Chenin Blanc, 11% Verdelho, and 4% Muscat, all planted in 2010 at 360m elevation. 13% alcohol. Cost: $54. click to buy.

2024 Black Water “Rockview” Sauvignon Blanc, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of passionfruit, pink grapefruit, and honeysuckle. In the mouth, silky flavors of pink grapefruit and passionfruit are electric with amazing acidity and crystalline stony minerality. Amazingly bright. From 32-year-old vines. Barrel fermented and aged 10 months in oak. 13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2021 Craven Wines “Karibib Vineyard” Chenin Blanc, Polkadraai Hills, Stellenbosch, Western Cape, South Africa
Pale yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of grapefruit, pomelo, and hints of herb oil. In the mouth, electric acidity delivers unripe apple, quince, citrus oil, and citrus pith flavors with gorgeous saline brightness and juiciness. Yum! 12.5% alcohol. Cost: $32.

2024 Crystallum “Clay Shales” Chardonnay, Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, white flowers, struck match, and sea air. In the mouth, electric acidity and wonderfully salty lemon peel, lemon pith, and lemon oil are a neon burst of yellow light on the tongue. Fantastic acidity and wonderful stony minerality. Aged about 8 months in 20% new oak. 13.2% alcohol. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2024 Crystallum “Ferrum” Chardonnay, Overberg, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, lemon oil, candied pink grapefruit, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, wonderfully salty, crystalline flavors of pink grapefruit and lemon oil are zingy with fantastic acidity. Chalky, stony notes linger in the finish with grapefruit oil. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2024 Damascene “Moya Meaker” Chardonnay, Elgin, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, lemon curd, and lemon oil. In the mouth, silky flavors of lemon oil, white flowers, crushed stone, and a hint of nougat have gorgeous crystalline acidity. Fermented and aged for 11 months in a 1,000 L foudre. Malolactic conversion blocked. No sulfur until bottling. 13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Damascene “Moya Meaker” Riesling, Elgin, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of wet stones, elderflower, a hint of citrus pith, and white ginger. In the mouth, white ginger, wet stones, and citrus pith have a long, bright, stony wet chalkboard character. Fermented in concrete only. Malolactic conversion blocked. 5.5 g/L residual sugar. Perhaps the most impressive bottling of Riesling I’ve ever had from South Africa. 13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Damascene Sémillon, Franschhoek, Coastal Region, South Africa
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, lemon pith, wet chalkboard, and yellow herbs. In the mouth, intense lemon and yellow herb flavors are backed by a chalky, bright, stony, deeply mineral character with an amazing crushed-stone quality. Fermented and aged in a 1,000 L foudre. Malolactic conversion blocked. From sandstone soils with vines planted in 1952 and 1962. 13% alcohol. Cost: $45. click to buy.

2021 Damascene Sémillon, Franschhoek, Western Cape, South Africa
Pale yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of candied lemon peel, lemon oil, and white flowers. In the mouth, gorgeous mineral, saline flavors of candied lemon peel, white flowers, and wet pavement are silky yet deeply mineral. Outstanding. From 1942 plantings. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $45.

2024 FRAM Chenin Blanc, Piekenierskloof, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, pear skin, and hints of fynbos. In the mouth, saline flavors of pear skin, bee pollen, elderflower, and aromatic herbs are gorgeously bright and juicy with fantastic acidity. Deeply mineral. From 520 m elevation. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $34. click to buy.

NV FRAM “Carmelina” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of roasted nuts, dried herbs, and exotic citrus peel. In the mouth, salty citrus peel, crushed roasted nuts, white sage, and wet chalkboard flavors have gorgeous acidity and chalky minerality. Distinctive and delicious. A blend of mostly Palomino and a few other varieties from the 2020, 2021, and 2022 vintages. 12% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Gabriëlskloof “Landscape Series – Era René” Chenin Blanc, Bot River, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear and white flowers. In the mouth, honeysuckle, Asian pear, wet chalkboard, and white tea flavors have a wonderful crystalline brightness and pear skin bitterness in the finish. Fantastic acidity and clarity. Excellent.13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Gabriëlskloof “Landscape Series – Elodie” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in color, this wine smells of pear, white melon, pomelo, and white flowers. In the mouth, saline, electric grapefruit pith, Asian pear, and pear skin flavors mix with a deeply mineral crushed-stone quality. Chalky, bright, and mouthwatering. Outstanding.13% alcohol. Cost: $38. click to buy.

2021 Miles Mossop Wines “Chapter Three” Chenin Blanc, Stellenbosch, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of intense citrus oil and crushed stones. In the mouth, gorgeously saline flavors of lemon oil, pear, grapefruit, crushed stones, and pomelo linger beautifully. 13.5% alcohol. 1,510 bottles made. Cost: $??

2021 Miles Mossop Wines “Chapter Four” Sauvignon Blanc, Stellenbosch, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of green apple and herbs. In the mouth, gorgeous stony passionfruit, lemon pith, dried herbs, and crushed-stone notes have fantastically bright acidity. Fabulous salinity and brightness. Delicious.13.5% alcohol. Cost: $??

2023 Momento Grenache Blanc, Western Cape, South Africa
Light gold in the glass with a hint of bronze, this wine smells of white peach, nectarine, lemon pith, and a hint of floral melon. In the mouth, crackling acidity and wet chalkboard minerality underlie white nectarine, lemon pith, and green apple flavors. Crystalline and gorgeous, with faint salinity. Two days of skin contact before aging in neutral oak. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $34. click to buy.

2023 Momento “Chenin Blanc Verdelho” White Blend, Western Cape, South Africa
Light gold in the glass with a hint of bronze, this wine smells of lemon oil, lemon blossom, beeswax, and bee pollen. In the mouth, electric lemon and bee pollen flavors mix with pink grapefruit, a hint of Asian pear, and pear skin. Fantastic acidity and minerality. A blend of 63% Chenin Blanc and 37% Verdelho. Whole-cluster pressed into old oak. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $213. click to buy. (I have NO idea why this is so expensive in the US).

2024 Rall Grenache Blanc, Piekenierskloof, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of white peaches, apples, and white flowers. In the mouth, zingy green apple, white peach, and guava notes are wonderfully saline and crunchy, with mouthwatering acidity and a faint tannic grip. Gorgeous. Fermented in concrete. 12% alcohol. 404 bottles made. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2024 Rall White Blend, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of honeysuckle, beeswax, pear, and elderflower. In the mouth, saline, juicy flavors of lemon pith, grapefruit, Asian pear, and wet stone are electric with gorgeous acidity. Beautiful and crystalline in quality. A blend of Chenin Blanc, Verdelho, and a touch of Viognier, aged in a variety of vessels. 13% alcohol. Cost: $30. click to buy.

2024 Rall “AVA” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest blonde in the glass, this wine smells of pear skin and Bosc pear with a hint of dried herbs. In the mouth, electric pear and pear skin, grapefruit, pomelo pith, white sage, crushed stones, and wet chalkboard flavors have great acidity and impressive length. Fermented in foudre over the course of more than a year. 12.5% alcohol. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2021 Savage Wines “Never Been Asked to Dance” Chenin Blanc, Paarl, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of grapefruit pith and grapefruit juice. In the mouth, electrically bright, mineral, crystalline flavors of lemon, grapefruit, quince, and crushed stones linger with yellow herbs through a very long, saline finish. Delicious. From vines planted in 1956. Cost: $50. click to buy.

2021 Savage Wines “Not Tonight Josephine” Chenin Blanc, Piekenierskloof, Western Cape, South Africa
Light amber in the glass, this wine smells of honey and marmalade. In the mouth, incredibly bright honey, marmalade, candied orange peel, orange blossom water, and orange blossom honey flavors are moderately to very sweet and have a positively electric acidity with great length and persistence. 250 litres made per year. 400 g/L residual sugar. 7.5% alcohol. Cost: $??

White, Pink, and Orange Wines With a Score Between 9 and 9.5

2024 Alheit Vineyards “Cartology” Chenin Blanc, Western Cape, South Africa
Bright yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, white flowers, and citrus pith. In the mouth, lean and bright citrus pith, pear, and a hint of yellow flowers mix with lovely acidity and nice wet pavement minerality. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $66. click to buy.

2023 Alheit Vineyards “Cartology” Chenin Blanc, Western Cape, South Africa
Near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of grapefruit, wet chalkboard, and lemon peel. In the mouth, stony wet chalkboard, saline grapefruit, and lemon flavors have wonderful brightness and excellent acidity. Contains 6% Sémillon. Cost: $58. click to buy.

2023 Black Water “High Roller” Sauvignon Blanc, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers and grapefruit oil. In the mouth, gorgeous pink grapefruit, wet stones, and white-flower flavors have a faint salinity, gorgeous chalky texture, and fantastic acidity. Stony, with amazing purity of candied pink grapefruit. Fermented entirely in stainless steel. 13% alcohol. Cost: $16. click to buy.

2022 Black Water “Pleasure Garden” Palomino, Robertson, Breede River Valley, South Africa
Light to medium gold in the glass, this wine smells of yellow herbs, crushed nuts, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, yellow herbs, nut skin, saltwater, and dried cooking herb flavors have a lovely briny, salty note that is very compelling. Deeply stony, with a chalky texture and great length. 11.8% alcohol. Cost: $21. click to buy.

2021 Craven Wines Chardonnay, Polkadraai Hills, Stellenbosch, Western Cape, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon curd, lemon pith, and lemon juice. In the mouth, saline lemon pith, grapefruit, and a touch of herbs mix with wet chalkboard and a nice lemon peel note. Excellent acidity. 11.5% alcohol. Cost: $32. click to buy.

2022 Craven Wines Pinot Gris, Stellenbosch, Western Cape, South Africa
Light rosy ruby in the glass, this wine smells of berries and wet leaves. In the mouth, wet leaves, berries, and citrus peel flavors mix with nice wet pavement minerality. Lovely chalky grip in the finish with excellent acidity. Destemmed into concrete, punched down, fermented to dryness on the skins, and then returned to concrete for five to six months. 12% alcohol. Cost: $17. click to buy.

2024 Crystallum “Agnes” Chardonnay, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon peel, lemon pith, and a hint of grapefruit. In the mouth, saline flavors of lemon peel, pink grapefruit, pomelo pith, and dried herbs have excellent acidity with a light chalky grip. 13.5% alcohol. 36 barrels made. Cost: $45. click to buy.

2021 Damascene “Moya Meaker” Riesling, Elgin, Western Cape, South Africa
Palest greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of mandarin oils and wet chalkboard. content:
Hello and welcome to my weekly dig through the pile of wine samples that show up on my doorstep asking to be tasted. I’m pleased to bring you the latest installment of Vinography Unboxed, where I highlight some of the better bottles that have arrived recently.

This past week I received a few new releases from Spur Road Wines, a wine project by Sam and Amanda Buckingham a couple who are assistant winemakers by day, but in their spare time revitalizing the Nozzari vineyard on the Sonoma Coast in their spare time. When they took over the vineyard, it was neglected and overgrown with blackberry bushes. Now it’s making some pretty interesting wines. They sent along their very competent and tasty white Pinot Noir along with its inverse twin, which I enjoyed but not quite as much as the blanc version. Their GFG single-vineyard bottling was also good, along with their Sonoma Coast blend. This is an interesting young label to watch, for sure.

I also received a bunch of recent releases from Waits-Mast Cellars, a project that I have watched grow from its very infancy into the established and reliably excellent producer that it is today. Jennifer Waits and Brian Mast lived in my neighborhood in San Francisco, and I would see them at the local community wine parties I threw every few months as a way of giving away wine samples. They eventually brought along a bottle they had just made at an urban custom crush facility in San Francisco, and continued to show me their increasingly serious efforts over the years. These days they employ winemaker Shalini Sekhar and source fruit from some of the top vineyards in Anderson Valley. My favorites this week were their interpretations of the Nash Mill and Oppenlander vineyards, but all four wines they sent me were delicious.

Last but not least, I got a chance to taste the latest Cabernet Sauvignon from Mayacamas Vineyards which is just being released by the winery. Their 2022 shows the estate’s characteristic restraint in ripeness and oak usage, while also nicely avoiding any signs of what was a pretty hot vintage. The wine is smooth, energetic, and wonderfully balanced. If you like old-school styling in your Cabernet Sauvignon, with potential for long ageability, Mayacamas is still a very good buy, even as it gets more expensive.

Notes on all these wines below.

Tasting Notes

2025 Spur Road “Nozzari Vineyard” White Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Palest straw to the point of being near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, citrus peel, and yellow raspberries. In the mouth, bright berry and citrus pith flavors have a nice snap to them thanks to excellent acidity. There’s a light herbal note here as well, adding complexity as the mouth waters. 12.8% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $35. click to buy.

2024 Spur Road “Nozzari Vineyard” Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in color, this wine smells of cranberries, cherries, chopped green herbs, and a touch of forest floor. In the mouth, powdery, gauzy tannins drape around a core of forest floor, cranberries, raspberries, and dried herbs. There’s a hint of bitter orange peel in the finish. Excellent acidity. 13.2% alcohol. 50 cases made. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $58. click to buy.

2024 Spur Road Pinot Noir, Sonoma Coast, Sonoma, California
Medium garnet in the glass with a faint haze, this wine smells of wet earth, chopped green herbs, and lettuce with a hint of berries. In the mouth, savory and earthy notes of raspberries and pomegranate seeds have a faint sawdust quality and dusty tannins. Very good acidity. A hint of sawdust and vanilla linger in the finish. 12.8% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $47.

Light to medium garnet in color, this wine smells of wet earth, raspberries, and chopped aromatic herbs. Morning light rakes across the front of the hill of Somló, highlighting one of the hundreds of small buildings that winemakers often have in their vineyards. These structures, which range from huts to more substantial homes, often have no electricity or running water, and are used both practically and for pleasure. They’re an easy place to get out of a rainstorm, but also a great place for picnics and weekend respites when the weather is nice. As almost all the winemakers in this little Hungarian wine region live at some distance from the hill itself, they’re also someplace to crash after the end of a long day in the vineyard.

content:
No one, including me, pays enough attention to Santa Barbara Wine Country. It’s frankly one of the greatest sources of California Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, but somehow seems to take a back seat compared to the glitz and glamour of Northern California wine country.

Want to see what you’re missing? Then you might want to check out the Wine and Fire Festival put on by the Sta. Rita Hills Wine Alliance. In this time of climate disasters and crazy fires, I’m not so sure about the name they chose for the event (let’s hope there are NO fires), but I am sure that it will be a fantastic opportunity to taste some incredible Pinot and Chardonnay, eat some fantastic food, and spend time learning, drinking, and celebrating with wine lovers and winemakers alike.

The weekend begins on Thursday, August 13th, with several seminars and tastings. That evening there’s a Barn Party at Sanford and Benedict Winery. Friday sports more seminars and tastings, culminating in the Grand Tasting on Saturday, August 15th from 4:00 to 7:00. The Grand Tasting, which takes place at the historic La Purisima Mission, will feature live music and lots of food offerings from local purveyors “showcasing grilled, roasted, and smoked specialties alongside curated seasonal bites,” according to the event website. Sounds pretty tasty to me!

The wineries participating and pouring at the main event include: 10 Ninths, Alma Rosa Winery & Vineyards, Ampelos Cellars, Babcock Winery, Brewer-Clifton, Caella Wines, Camins 2 Dreams, Clementine Carter, Colluvial, Cotiere Winery, Dierberg Vineyard, Donnachadh Family Wines, Dragonette, Evan’s Ranch Estate Vineyard, Fiddlehead Cellars, Flying Goat Cellars, Gainey Estate Vineyard, Hitching Post Wines, Holus Bolus, Ken Brown Wines, Kessler-Haak Wines, Liquid Farm, Longoria Wines, Loubud Wines, MarBeso, Melville Winery, Montemar Wines, Pali Wine Co., Piazza Family Wines, SAMsARA Wine Co., Sanford Winery & Vineyards, Sea Smoke, Seagrape Wine Co., Spear Vineyards & Winery, Story of Soil, Sweetzer Cellars, Tercero Wines, The Joy Fantastic, The Ojai Vineyard, The Set, Tomi Cellars, Tyler Winery, and William Hines Wines.

Tickets are going fast for the event, so make your plans!

2026 Sta. Rita Hills Wine & Fire Festival
Grand Tasting Saturday, August 15th 4:00 PM – 7:00 PM
La Purisima Mission State Historic Park
2295 Purisima Rd
Lompoc, CA 93436 (map)

Tickets for the seminars and tastings, including the Grand Tasting, are $156 and change. The Barn Party will run you around $125. Shuttle service is also available for a fee from local hotels (highly recommended both to avoid parking hassles and keep everyone safe). All tickets should be purchased online in advance as they will likely sell out. Some of the individual seminars and vertical tastings are already sold out. Dress carefully and bring layers, as it could be warm to start and then quite chilly as the breeze moves in.

Leave it to the NYT to sensationalize the headline. The burning is incidental to the ripping out.

Jancis on Georgia.

No good and very bad.

A better way to offer a “where to buy” link on your website.

Guides are out, says Andy Neather.

The Dottie and John guide to corkage.

Today’s modernists are tomorrow’s classics.

A very long trial of screwcaps from a leading Napa winery.

I’m not watching the fine signals amidst the noise, but this seems like a too-early optimism to me.

Yes, but the biggest players won’t buy in (ahem: Gallo).

Croatia on the rise, apparently.

Pray for good winds, people.

A wine writer can’t escape wine country.

THE legend of Abruzzo. RIP.

A family returns to their pioneering vineyard.

I Studied Wine for 12 Weeks. It Taught Me the Skills AI Can’t Replace
Cultivate beginner’s mind.

Winery that rose from the ashes of Napa wildfire faces foreclosure 2 years after reopening
Youch. That was a short-lived renaissance.

Hot Weather Plagues French Harvest
Prayers to the rain gods are myriad.

Meet the Barolo Masters Betting Big on Barbaresco
Used to be the affordable Nebbiolo. Not much longer.

What Else Do We Lose When People Give Up Booze?
Togetherness, for one.

How Wineries Are Reinventing the Tasting Room Experience
Not just bellying up to the bar anymore.

An Israeli Partnership Helps Tanzania Grow Its Wine Industry
Love the collaboration.

title: The Taste of Carbon Neutrality: International Wineries for Climate Action
summary:
The wine world is full of organizations and associations, spanning a wide range of missions, purposes, and themes. Only a

The post The Taste of Carbon Neutrality: International Wineries for Climate Action appeared first on Vinography.
content:
The wine world is full of organizations and associations, spanning a wide range of missions, purposes, and themes. Only a few, however, are focused on saving the planet. One of those, International Wineries for Climate Action, came to Napa earlier in the year to offer a tasting they billed as the largest tasting of low-emission wines ever held in Napa.

I didn’t know much about the IWCA before the tasting. I had read headlines and an occasional article about the group, but was vague on the details. After this tasting and a deep dive into what they’re doing, I consider them one of the most impressive wine organizations on the planet.

Founded by Familia Torres and Jackson Family Wines in 2019, the organization was launched to create a community of wineries dedicated to reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the wine lifecycle towards a goal of complete carbon neutrality. The idea being that in collaboration and with shared purpose, wineries can do more, faster, than if they each go at it alone.

That sounds like a pretty good idea, right? But once you have the idea, you very quickly become faced with the question of how the heck to do that effectively and efficiently, and more specifically, you have to figure out what to focus on first.

And that is a lot harder than it sounds.

In order to know where to focus, you need to know where you stand, which involves something called carbon accounting. Basically, you need to measure and/or calculate your carbon footprint as a wine business across the entirety of the wine lifecycle: planting, farming, winemaking, packaging, marketing, sales, hospitality, waste, business operations, and energy use, to name just a few of the areas that make up your average winery’s carbon footprint. Within each of those areas there are dozens and dozens of factors that have an emissions impact.

That’s why the Torres and Jackson families began their work by creating a set of comprehensive carbon emission calculators for the wine industry, which they make available for free on the IWCA.Org website for anyone to use. You know the old business adage: you can’t manage what you can’t measure? That’s the idea here.

To even apply to be a member of the IWCA, you must have done the calculations to measure your internal, direct greenhouse gas emissions and energy usage, and you must have a plan to measure your external emissions footprint (e.g. everything purchased outside and brought into the winery) and get the measurements audited by a third party.

Accepted members have a year to reach Silver status, at which they commit to reaching Net-Zero carbon footprint by 2050, intermediate targets by 2030, and have begun to follow the international emissions reduction protocols that the group has adopted. Those members who achieve 20% renewable self-generation of energy and measurable ongoing emissions reductions per liter of wine produced annually can graduate to Gold membership, which 18 of the 49 members have now done.

“We’re very proud of the fact that since our founding a little more than six years ago we’ve grown to more than 49 companies, which encompass 175 wineries across 14 countries,” says Katie Jackson of Jackson Family Wines. “The group accounts for about 3.5% of total global wine emissions. When we started, Miguel’s [Torres] goal was really to get to that 5%. Once we’re at 50 members plus, we really start to make an impact.”

Crucially, the emissions reduction protocols adopted by the group involve no carbon offsets whatsoever, which are problematic for various reasons.

“What sets us apart from many climate-focused organizations in the wine business is that our members are being asked to make reductions themselves, to take actions that make real, meaningful change,” says Jackson.

That change takes place in a multitude of obvious and non-obvious ways. The obvious things involve making fewer tractor passes in the vineyard, using lighter-weight glass bottles, and managing CO2 usage in the winemaking process. Non-obvious things involve things so obscure that many people might not even consider them, such as the carbon footprint of throwing away the thousands of pounds of backing release film that all bottle labels are spooled onto.

Several of the Sonoma and Napa winery members have joined the North Bay Zero Waste Collective, an organization that, among other things, allows them to pool their waste products to achieve economies of scale that allow for re-use and recycling of materials such as the ubiquitous stretch film that surrounds anything shipped on a pallet.

“We all have pallets coming in with stretch film, and we’re all sending out pallets with stretch film. So what do we do with this?” says Brooke Shenk, Winemaker at St. Supery Vineyards. “We came up with a reuse process for large amounts of stretch film and have partnered with a company that bought it all and turned it back into stretch film.”

This local North Bay group has diverted 244,000 pounds of materials from ending up in a landfill over the last couple of years.

This is precisely the power of collective action that the IWCA was founded to both inspire and achieve, and the results are impressive.

The accomplishments of the current 49 members of the IWCA are impressive. A to Z Wineworks in Oregon reduced their water usage 33% from one year to the next, saving 8 metric tons of CO2 emissions. Château Tour des Termes built the first LEED-Certified wine cellar in France. Château Troplong Mondot has figured out how to use its vine pruning waste to heat its buildings in the winter, saving an incredible amount of emissions every year. Familia Torres is up to 55% self-generated electricity and achieved a 38% reduction in their bottle weights. St. Supery Vineyards is 80% solar powered and has reduced water usage by 56% over 8 years. Symington Family Estates has reduced their glass-related carbon footprint from 30% of total emissions to 24% of emissions over 5 years. Viñas Familia Gil has achieved true zero-waste status as a winery. Henschke has reduced their emissions intensity by 37% since 2022.

It’s a shame that there aren’t more wineries involved. Granted, the effort required to even just do the calculations required for membership application is no small feat. Such efforts might be inconceivable for small family wineries. But there are plenty of mid-sized wineries with the staff and resources to do these kinds of audits. And frankly, it’s the larger players in the industry (with the corresponding largest emissions) that can make the most impact in greenhouse gas reduction.

Irrespective of the high bar for membership, IWCA has created a set of tools and resources that can allow any winery interested in understanding and making positive progress on their carbon footprint to do so.

There’s no excuse for any winery not to get started.

Tasting Notes

These wines are all made by IWCA member wineries and are arranged in descending order of score. You can purchase these wines knowing that you are supporting a company that has made meaningful, measurable progress towards saving the planet. If that doesn’t taste good, I don’t know what does.

2021 Henschke “Mount Edelstone” Shiraz, Eden Valley, South Australia, Australia
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of crushed rocks, struck match, and black olives. In the mouth, black cherry and black olive flavors have supple, fine tannins and great acidity. Long, incredibly smooth, and balanced. A stunner of a wine. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $290. click to buy.

Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherry, blackcurrant, flowers, and a hint of espresso. In the mouth, black cherries, espresso, flowers, and blackberry flavors have supple, fleecy tannins, great acidity, and a very long finish with a hint of sweet oak. Beautiful. 13.7% alcohol. Score: around 9.5. Cost: $280. click to buy.

Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherry, flowers, and graphite. In the mouth, muscular, fine tannins squeeze black cherry, green herbs, and graphite, with a hint of espresso. Refined. 14% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $452. click to buy.

Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of blackberries, blueberries, herbs, and plums. In the mouth, muscular tannins surround flavors of blackberries, blueberries, herbs, and dried plums. Long and fine-grained tannins are matched with great acidity. Lovely. 14.4% alcohol. Score: between 9 and 9.5. Cost: $54. click to buy.

Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherry, coconut, and dried herbs. In the mouth, black cherry and dried herb flavors are wrapped in tight, fleecy tannins. Good acidity, nice length, supple, and smooth. 14.6% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $78. click to buy.

2019 Château Troplong Mondot Bordeaux Blend, Saint-Émilion, Bordeaux, France
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of graphite, truffle, and blackcurrants. In the mouth, juicy blackcurrant and blackcurrant leaf flavors mix with green herbs. Fine tannins, great acidity, and nice length. A blend of 85% Merlot, 13% Cabernet Sauvignon, and 2% Cabernet Franc. Little sensory trace of its 15% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $125. click to buy.

2021 Frog’s Leap Winery Cabernet Sauvignon, Rutherford, Napa, California
Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, earth, and graphite. In the mouth, black cherry flavors and a hint of blackcurrant are wrapped in fleecy tannins. Very good acidity and nice weight. Contains 9% Cabernet Franc. 14% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $70. click to buy.

Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of apples, pears, and vanilla. In the mouth, crisp green apple, Asian pear, and melon flavors have very good acidity and a long, chalky finish. Very pretty. 12.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $26. click to buy.

Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of floral strawberries and forest berries. In the mouth, juicy strawberry and boysenberry flavors are wrapped in fleecy tannins, with excellent acidity, and a long finish. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $40. click to buy.

Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon curd, roasted nuts, and struck match. In the mouth, saline lemon curd flavors are lean, juicy, stony, and tight. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 9. Cost: $147. click to buy.

2022 Kir-Yianni “Cuvée Villages” Xinomavro, Naoussa, Macedonia, Greece
Light to medium ruby in the glass, this wine smells of berries, including cranberries, and herbs. In the mouth, cranberry, sour cherry, and unripe blackberry flavors are wrapped in tight, muscular tannins. Great acidity. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $19. click to buy.

Medium ruby in the glass with garnet highlights, this wine smells of strawberries, chopped herbs, and earth. In the mouth, strawberry and earth flavors have lightly grippy tannins and excellent acidity. A hint of orange peel lingers on the finish. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $20. click to buy.

2023 Neleman Wines “Casas del Rey – Robusta” Bobal, Utiel-Requena, Valencia, Spain
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of struck match, black cherry, and earth. In the mouth, black cherry and earth flavors have tight, fleecy tannins and good acidity. Dark in character. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $20.

2020 Château Tour des Termes Bordeaux Blend, Saint-Estèphe, Bordeaux, France
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cassis and graphite with a hint of cigar box. In the mouth, lean flavors of cigar box and blackcurrant have fine tannins, a supple texture, and very good acidity. Savory. A blend of 50% Merlot, 40% Cabernet Sauvignon, 5% Cabernet Franc, and 5% Petit Verdot. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $40. click to buy.

2020 Familia Torres “Mas La Plana” Cabernet Sauvignon, Penedès, Catalonia, Spain
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of dried herbs and dark berries. In the mouth, cherry and berry fruit flavors mix with orange peel, framed by tight, fine-grained tannins and great acidity. 14.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $105. click to buy.

2017 CVNE “Viña Real Gran Reserva Especial” Rioja, Spain
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, sawdust, and dried herbs. In the mouth, tight tannins surround flavors of cherry, orange peel, earth, and leather. Sawdust notes and very good acidity linger in the finish. A blend of 95% Tempranillo and 5% Graciano. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $67. click to buy.

Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon pith and pears layered over wet chalkboard. In the mouth, wet pavement, yellow herbs, and lemon pith flavors are crisp and bright with very good acidity. 12% alcohol. Score: between 8.5 and 9. Cost: $15. click to buy.

Light to medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of oak, cherry, and cranberries. In the mouth, cherries, cranberries, oak, and dried herb flavors are dominated by wood, with a hint of struck match. Decent acidity. 13.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $22. click to buy.

2022 Juan Gil “Silver Label” Monastrell, Jumilla, Murcia, Spain
Medium to dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of black cherries, blueberries, and herbs. In the mouth, black cherry, floral, and blueberry flavors have great acidity and tight tannins. 14.5% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $15. click to buy.

2019 Cakebread Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California

Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of passionfruit and gooseberries. In the mouth, gooseberry, green apple, and cut grass flavors have bright acidity. Zingy and lean. 13% alcohol. Score: around 8.5. Cost: $23. click to buy.

2023 Domaine Bousquet “Virgen” Malbec, Tupungato, Uco Valley, Mendoza, Argentina
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of cherries, oak, and earth. In the mouth, a narrow core of cherry mixes with sawdust, earth, and licorice, framed by fine, tight tannins. Feels somewhat compressed. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $13. click to buy.

Medium garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raspberries, cranberries, and herbs. In the mouth, cranberries, herbs, and orange peel flavors have tight, fine tannins and good acidity. 13.5% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $28. click to buy.

2023 St. Supéry “Napa Valley Estate” Cabernet Sauvignon, Napa Valley, Napa, California
Dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of mocha and black cherry. In the mouth, drying, fleecy tannins frame cherry and dried herb flavors, while sweet oak competes for attention. Good acidity, but the overall effect feels overdone. 14.5% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $65. click to buy.

Very dark garnet in the glass, this wine smells of raisins, chocolate, and stewed black cherries. In the mouth, fleecy tannins wrap around sweet stewed black cherry, licorice, and blueberry flavors. Decent acidity. A blend of Touriga Franca, Touriga Nacional, Tinta Roriz, and Tinta Barroca. 19.5% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $27. click to buy.

2019 Miguel Torres “VIGNO” Carignan, Maule, Chile

In the mouth, struck match, boysenberry, and blueberry flavors are juicy but very high-toned, leaving the wine feeling a little hollow. Very good acidity. 14% alcohol. Score: between 8 and 8.5. Cost: $23. click to buy.
